query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor fraction of silver to the high-entropy alloy will enable the in‐situ formation of a lubricious, self‐healing oxide nanocomposite (tribolayer) during sliding that reduces both the friction coefficient and wear rate over a broad temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional high-entropy alloy (HEA) lacking silver, which under sliding exhibits relatively high metal–metal contact, friction, and wear due to unmitigated asperity interactions and less-protective native oxide layers.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a controlled, minor amount of silver (e.g., on the order of 10–15 at% as demonstrated in alloys like (TiNbZr)75Ag25) into the HEA during synthesis.
generation.conditions: Tribological sliding in ambient air across a wide service-temperature range (from room temperature up to elevated temperatures, e.g., 600 °C), with the material functioning as a self‐lubricating surface under typical mechanical loads.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an in‐situ, amorphous–crystalline oxide/tribolayer enriched with dispersed silver nanocrystals at the worn surface.
generation.mechanism: During sliding, the presence of Ag facilitates reactive wear protection by promoting oxidation and segregation at the contact interface. This leads to the development of a continuous, low-shear tribolayer that minimizes direct asperity contact. The tribolayer reduces friction and wear via a combination of lubricious oxide formation and self-healing surface reconstruction.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated HEA, the Ag-alloyed HEA is predicted to show a substantial (e.g., 30–70%) reduction in coefficient of friction and a significant (potentially up to two orders of magnitude) decrease in wear rate across the entire tested temperature range.
generation.baseline: The untreated high-entropy alloy without Ag exhibits higher friction and wear, with less stable oxide formation under sliding conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect may be diminished in oxygen‐deficient environments or at temperatures outside the stability range of the reactive tribolayer. The precise optimal Ag content and processing conditions also need further exploration.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative improvement is supported by evidence of reactive wear protection in similar systems, the exact quantitative reduction in friction and wear, as well as the optimal Ag level, remain to be fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples that are identical except for the incorporation of a minor amount of Ag in one set. Subject both sets to standardized ball-on-disk sliding experiments in ambient air over a range of temperatures (from room temperature to ~600 °C) with identical loads and sliding distances. Monitor friction behavior and conduct post-test wear track analysis.
measurements: Coefficient of friction measured in real time using a tribometer
Wear rate determination via 3D optical profilometry of the wear tracks
Surface characterization of the worn regions using SEM/EDS and Raman spectroscopy to assess tribolayer formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ag-alloyed samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in friction (less than ~30% improvement) and wear rate (less than an order-of-magnitude improvement) relative to the baseline HEA over the tested temperature range, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

The comprehensive post‐test characterizations coupled with MD simulation studies revealed interesting tribochemistry at play leading to the dissociation of entrapped ethanol molecules and converting it into a‐C in the presence of catalytically active HEA nanoflakes, which are responsible for the formation of tribolayer, wherein the full lubricious behavior was complemented by the retained HEA nanoflakes. This discovery opens up a new avenue to develop advanced solid lubricants based on 2D HEA with high compositional flexibility and low‐shear‐strength layered structure for oil‐free tribological systems. The other important aspect of the 2D HEA lubricant developed in this study is the ability to coat the given surface using a simple spray coating technique. Wear-related energy and material loss cost over 2500 Billion Euro per year. Traditional wisdom suggests that high-strength materials reveal low wear rates, yet, their plastic deformation mechanisms also influence their wear performance. High strength and homogeneous deformation behavior, which allow accommodating plastic strain without cracking or localized brittle fracture, are crucial for developing wear-resistant metals. Here, we present an approach to achieve superior wear resistance via in-situ formation of a strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surface during wear, by reaction of the metal surface with its oxidative environment, a principle that we refer to as ‘reactive wear protection’. We design a TiNbZr-Ag alloy that forms an amorphous-crystalline oxidic nanocomposite surface layer upon dry sliding. The strong (2.4 GPa yield strength) and deformable (homogeneous deformation to 20% strain) nanocomposite surface reduces the wear rate of the TiNbZr-Ag alloy by an order of magnitude.
